slides.title: Detection - Single Instance
slides.body: Detection - Single Instance

slides.title: Why Detect Deadlocks At All?
slides.body:
OS Lets Deadlock Happen, Then Finds It
No prevention, no avoidance, deadlock can occur
OS periodically checks system state for deadlock
Goal: Detect deadlock, then recover from it
Many OS grant requests immediately, unlike Banker's Algorithm which checks safety first
slides.notes: Alright, so far we've seen how deadlocks can be prevented or avoided. Now we'll look at a different approach where the operating system doesn't try to stop deadlocks from happening. Instead, it grants resource requests immediately without performing safety checks, allowing deadlocks to occur if they do. The operating system then periodically checks the system for deadlocks, and if one is detected, it takes appropriate steps to recover from it.

slides.title: Why Detect Deadlocks At All?
slides.body: OS Lets Deadlock Happen, Then Finds It
slides.notes: Next, let's compare deadlock avoidance and deadlock detection based on when the operating system takes action. In avoidance, every resource request is checked before it is granted to ensure the system remains safe. In detection, requests are granted immediately, and the operating system checks for deadlocks after the resources have already been allocated. This difference is what makes the two approaches fundamentally different.

slides.title: Deadlock Detection Approach
slides.body:
Analogy
Analogy: Like a housing society with no security guard checking visitors at the gate, residents move freely; only later does the watchman do rounds and spot a locked-in mess, exactly like the OS checking for deadlock after allocation.
slides.notes: Analogy: Like a housing society with no security guard checking visitors at the gate, residents move freely; only later does the watchman do rounds and spot a locked-in mess, exactly like the OS checking for deadlock after allocation.

slides.title: Wait-For Graph for Single-Instance Resources
slides.body:
Collapsing the Resource-Allocation Graph
Built from Resource-Allocation Graph (RAG), resource nodes removed
Nodes represent only processes, not resources
Edge Pi to Pj means Pi waits for Pj
Drawn only when each resource has one instance
slides.notes:
Moving on, for systems where each resource type has only one instance, deadlock detection becomes even simpler using a Wait-For Graph. It is derived from the Resource Allocation Graph by removing all resource nodes, leaving only processes as nodes. An edge from Pi to Pj indicates 
that Pi is waiting for Pj to release a resource. This simplified graph makes deadlock detection much easier in single-instance resource systems.

slides.title: Single Instance
slides.body:
Cycle Is Necessary and Sufficient
Theorem: deadlock exists iff a cycle exists
Run depth-first search to find cycles
Maintain graph, re-check on each blocked request
Detection cost: O(n²), n = number of processes
slides.notes: Next, deadlock detection becomes very straightforward in a Wait-For Graph. The key theorem states that a deadlock exists if and only if a cycle exists in the graph. The operating system can use a Depth-First Search (DFS) to detect these cycles, typically checking the graph whenever a process becomes blocked. This detection process has a time complexity of O(n²), where n is the number of processes.

slides.title: Single Instance
slides.body: Cycle Is Necessary and Sufficient
slides.notes: Finally, interpreting the result is straightforward. If the Wait-For Graph contains no cycle, the system is deadlock-free because no processes are waiting in a circular chain. However, if a cycle exists, then every process involved in that cycle is deadlocked, as each one is waiting for another process in the same loop to release a resource.
tables: Every process in cycle is deadlocked
Every process in cycle is deadlocked

slides.title: Detection - Multiple Instances
slides.body: Detection - Multiple Instances

slides.title: Cycle ≠ Deadlock
slides.body:
Multiple Instances Change The Rule
With multiple instances of a resource type, a cycle in the graph no longer guarantees deadlock
Example: 2 printers shared among 3 processes
A cycle can exist, yet one instance may still free up
Cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock
Wait-for graph cannot be used here
slides.notes: Moving on, the situation changes when resource types have multiple instances. In this case, a cycle alone does not guarantee a deadlock because another instance of the resource may still become available and allow a waiting process to continue. So, while a cycle is necessary, it is not sufficient to conclude that a deadlock exists. This is why the Wait-For Graph approach cannot be used for systems with multiple resource instances.

slides.title: Detection Algorithm
slides.body:
Data Structures
This algorithm reuses the structure of  Safety Algorithm, but checks current pending Requests, not future Max needs
slides.notes: Now, let's look at the Deadlock Detection Algorithm for systems with multiple resource instances. It uses a structure very similar to the Safety Algorithm, but with one important difference.| Instead of checking a process's future maximum need, it works with the current pending Request of each process. The algorithm maintains three data structures:
tables: Instances each process is waiting for

slides.title: Deadlock Detection Steps
slides.body:
Check Whether Processes Complete
Work = Available; set Finish[i] = false if Allocation_i ≠ 0, else Finish[i] = true
A process holding no resources cannot be part of a deadlock, so it starts already finished
Pick i where Finish[i]=false and Request_i ≤ Work
slides.notes: Next, let's see how the Deadlock Detection Algorithm begins. It first sets Work = Available and initializes Finish[i] for every process. If a process has Allocation[i] = 0, it cannot be part of a deadlock, so Finish[i] is set to true. Otherwise, it starts as false. The algorithm then looks for a process with Finish[i] = false whose Request[i] ≤ Work, meaning its pending request can be satisfied.

slides.title: Deadlock Detection Steps
slides.body:
Work = Work + Allocation_i; set Finish[i] = true
Repeat until no such i exists
Any process with Finish[i]=false is deadlocked
Check Whether Processes Complete
slides.notes: Finally, whenever the algorithm finds such a process, it assumes the process completes, adds its allocated resources back to Work using Work = Work + Allocation[i], and marks Finish[i] = true. This process is repeated until no more processes can proceed. At the end, any process with Finish[i] = false is identified as deadlocked, since its request could never be satisfied.

slides.title: Worked Example: Five Processes, Three Resources
slides.body: Algorithm Step by Step
slides.notes:
Now, let's apply the Deadlock Detection Algorithm to a worked example. 
Since all resource instances are currently allocated, Available = Work = (0, 0, 0). Request[P0] = (0, 0, 0) 
can be satisfied immediately, so Finish[P0] becomes true, and its allocated resources are released, 
updating Work to (0, 1, 0). Even after this update, no other process has a Request ≤ Work,
 so P1, P2, P3, and P4 remain with Finish = false, indicating that they are deadlocked.

Work updates to (0,1,0) after adding P0's Allocation

Request[P0] = (0, 0, 0) can be satisfied immediately, so Finish[P0] becomes true, and its allocated resources are released, updating Work to (0, 1, 0). Even after this update, no other process has a Request ≤ Work, so P1, P2, P3, and P4 remain with Finish = false, indicating that they are deadlocked.

slides.title: Detection Frequency
slides.body: Detection Frequency

slides.title: Choosing Detection Frequency
slides.body:
Balance Overhead & Recovery Time
The detection algorithm itself costs CPU time, so it cannot run continuously. The OS must pick a sensible frequency
Detection algorithm costs O(m n²) per run
Running too often wastes CPU on healthy states
Running too rarely lets deadlocks persist longer
More entangled processes make recovery costlier later
slides.notes: Finally, the operating system must decide how often to run the Deadlock Detection Algorithm. Since each execution costs O(m × n²), running it too frequently wastes CPU time when the system is healthy. On the other hand, running it too infrequently allows deadlocks to persist longer, making recovery more difficult as more processes and resources become involved. The operating system therefore chooses a detection frequency that balances detection overhead with recovery cost.

slides.title: When Should Detection Actually Run?
slides.body:
Analogy
Analogy: Like an electrician checking wiring for a short: checking every minute wastes effort, checking once a month lets the fault spread.
slides.notes: Analogy: Like an electrician checking wiring for a short: checking every minute wastes effort, checking once a month lets the fault spread.

slides.title: Triggering Detection
slides.body:
Three Common Policies
Per-request detects deadlocks as soon as they occur
Infrequent checks may reveal many overlapping cycles
Utilisation drop is a practical real-system signal
slides.notes:
Finally, each detection policy has its own practical advantage. Per-request detection
 identifies deadlocks almost immediately, but it comes with the highest overhead. If the operating system checks only infrequently, it may discover multiple overlapping deadlocks at once, making recovery more complex. In real systems, a sudden drop in CPU utilisation is often used as a practical signal that many processes are blocked, prompting the operating system to run the deadlock detection algorithm.
tables: Run whenever a request cannot be granted
Run every fixed period, e.g. hourly
Run when CPU utilisation falls below a threshold, e.g. 40%
Runs only when system looks stuck

slides.title: Three Common Policies
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Like a factory inspecting its machines, the manager can inspect after every alarm (per-request policy), on a fixed schedule (fixed-interval policy), or only when production efficiency drops noticeably (utilisation-based policy). Similarly, an operating system decides when to run deadlock detection based on one of these three triggering policies.

slides.title: Recovering From a Confirmed Deadlock
slides.body:
Two Broad Recovery Methods
Heading: Recovering From a Confirmed Deadlock
Subheading: Two Broad Recovery Methods
Content:
Once detection confirms a deadlock, the OS must break the cycle. 
Once detection confirms a deadlock, the OS must break the cycle
slides.notes: Alright, once the operating system confirms that a deadlock exists, simply detecting it is not enough. The deadlock must be resolved so that the affected processes can continue execution. To achieve this, the operating system needs to break the circular wait by recovering from the deadlock. In the next few slides, we'll explore the two main recovery methods used to accomplish this.

slides.title: Recovering From a Confirmed Deadlock
slides.body:
Two Broad Recovery Methods
Deadlock Recovery

slides.title: Recovering From a Confirmed Deadlock
slides.body:
Two Broad Recovery Methods
Termination kills one or more deadlocked processes
Preemption snatches resources instead, covered next
Termination is simpler but destroys process work
slides.notes: Next, there are two main ways to recover from a deadlock. The first is process termination, where the operating system kills one or more deadlocked processes to break the circular wait. The second is resource preemption, where resources are taken away from selected processes without terminating them, which we'll discuss next. While termination is the simpler approach, it comes at the cost of losing the work already performed by the terminated processes.
tables: Kill every process in the cycle at once
Guarantees recovery, wastes all their work
Cheaper per step, needs repeated checks

slides.title: Recovering From a Confirmed Deadlock
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Like a group project stuck because members wait on each other: the teacher can disband the whole group, or remove one member at a time until work resumes.

slides.body:
Selection Criteria & Side Effects
Heading: Which Process Should Be Aborted?
Subheading: Selection Criteria & Side Effects
Content:
When aborting one process at a time, the OS picks a victim using cost-minimising criteria, similar to choosing a scheduling priority.
Process priority: lower-priority process chosen first
CPU time already consumed: less loss if aborted early
Resources held: prefer process holding fewer resources
Remaining work needed to finish: prefer far-from-done process
Process type: batch preferred over interactive process
Repeated selection of same process risks starvation

slides.notes: Next, if the operating system terminates one process at a time, it selects the victim based on the lowest recovery cost. Factors such as process priority, CPU time already used, resources held, remaining work, and process type are considered. Batch processes are usually preferred over interactive ones, and the operating system must avoid repeatedly aborting the same process to prevent starvation.

The operating system generally prefers terminating batch processes rather than interactive processes, since interactive applications directly affect the user experience. slides.title: Resource Preemption
slides.body:
Take Resource, Not Process
Selected process loses one held resource temporarily
Freed resource is handed to a blocked process
Instead of aborting a process, the OS may reclaim a safely preemptable resource from one process and allocate it to another process in the cycle
1
2
slides.notes: Next, instead of terminating a process, the operating system can use resource preemption to recover from a deadlock. In this approach, it temporarily takes a safely preemptable resource from one process and reallocates it to another blocked process in the deadlock cycle. This helps break the circular wait while allowing the affected processes to continue execution later.

slides.title: Resource Preemption
slides.body:
Cycle breaks without destroying the process itself
Three problems must be solved: victim, rollback, starvation
Instead of aborting a process, the OS may reclaim a safely preemptable resource from one process and allocate it to another process in the cycle.
3

Take Resource, Not Process
Instead of aborting a process, the OS may reclaim a safely preemptable resource from one process and allocate it to another process in the cycle
slides.notes: Finally, resource preemption breaks the deadlock without terminating any process by reclaiming a safely preemptable resource and assigning it to a blocked process. However, this approach introduces three important challenges: selecting the victim process, rolling back the affected process to a safe state, and preventing starvation if the same process is repeatedly chosen for preemption.

slides.title: Resource Preemption: Take the Resource, Not the Process
slides.body:
Analogy
Analogy: Like a library recalling a book from a reader before the due date to give it to a waitlisted student, the reader keeps their membership but temporarily loses the book.
slides.notes:
Like a library recalling a book from one reader to give it to a waitlisted student, 
the reader keeps their library membership but temporarily loses the book
. Similarly, in resource preemption, the operating system takes back a resource
 from one process and gives it to another, without terminating the process itself.

slides.title: Rollback: Restoring a Safe State
slides.body:
Total Rollback vs Partial Rollback
A process cannot simply resume after losing a resource mid-way; its computation may now be inconsistent

slides.notes: Moving on, when a process loses a resource through preemption, it cannot always continue from the same point because its computation may become inconsistent. Instead, the operating system performs a rollback, restoring the process to a previously saved safe state from which it can restart execution correctly. This rollback can be either total or partial, depending on how much of the process needs to be undone.

slides.notes: Next, to support rollback, the operating system periodically saves checkpoints of a process. If a recent checkpoint is available, the process can perform a partial rollback and resume from the last safe state before using the resource. Without checkpoints, only a total rollback is possible, restarting the process from the beginning. Rollback is also easier when the resource usage order is known in advance.

slides.title: Rollback: Restoring a Safe State
slides.body:
Analogy
Analogy: Like a cook who loses a borrowed ingredient midway through a recipe: with notes on each step, she redoes just the last step; without notes, she must restart the whole dish.
slides.notes: Like a cook who loses a borrowed ingredient midway through a recipe, she can redo only the last few steps if she has recipe notes (checkpoints). Without those notes, she must start the entire dish again. Similarly, rollback uses checkpoints for partial recovery; otherwise, a total rollback is required.

slides.title: Starvation
slides.body:
Same Process Keeps Losing Out
Heading: Starvation Under Repeated Preemption
Subheading: Making Sure One Process Doesn't Always Pay
Content:
A pure cost-minimising victim selection may repeatedly pick the same cheap process, so it never finishes its work.
Same low-cost process selected again on every cycle
That process keeps rolling back, never progressing
This is starvation, seen earlier with scheduling priorities
Fix: include preemption count in the cost function
Guarantee: a process can be preempted only a finite number of times
Same low-cost process selected again on every cycle
That process keeps rolling back, never progressing

Fix: include preemption count in the cost function
Guarantee: a process can be preempted only a finite number of times
A pure cost-minimising victim selection may repeatedly pick the same cheap process, so it never finishes its work.
A pure cost-minimising victim selection may repeatedly pick the same cheap process, so it never finishes its work
slides.notes: Finally, resource preemption can also lead to starvation if the operating system repeatedly selects the same low-cost process as the victim. That process keeps rolling back and may never finish its execution. To prevent this, the operating system includes the preemption count in its victim selection strategy, ensuring that no process is preempted an unlimited number of times.

slides.title: Starvation
slides.body: Same Process Keeps Losing Out
slides.notes: Next, the main cause of starvation is that the cost function ignores previous preemptions, so the same low-cost process keeps getting selected as the victim. A simple solution is to include the number of times a process has already been preempted in the cost calculation or reduce its chances of being selected after several preemptions. This ensures that every process eventually gets a fair opportunity to complete.

slides.title: Starvation
slides.body:
Analogy
Analogy: Like a cricket team's selectors always dropping the same player because he is easiest to replace, he never gets an innings to prove himself unless selectors factor in how often he was already dropped.
slides.notes: Like a cricket team that keeps dropping the same player because he is the easiest to replace, he never gets a chance to prove himself. Similarly, if the operating system always preempts the same low-cost process, it suffers starvation. To avoid this, the system considers how many times a process has already been preempted when selecting the next victim.
